Healthy food systems start with healthy soil. I build the infrastructure that returns food waste to it responsibly.Every year, enormous volumes of food are thrown away, much of it still in its packaging. Prevention and donation come first. But for the inedible food that remains, the choice is landfill, where it generates methane and wastes the nutrients and carbon it holds, or recycling into compost, renewable energy, and animal feed. Doing that well takes technology that can separate the food from the packaging without compromising what comes out the other end.At Denali, I develop food waste depackaging sites across the US, at Denali-owned and third-party composting, anaerobic digestion, and animal feed facilities. My work covers the full arc: site design, equipment evaluation, operating SOPs, and site management, with a focus on commingled source-separated organics from grocery stores. Denali collects and depackages tens of thousands of tons of inedible food per month, and I help site owners bring that capability to their own operations.I come to this from the operator’s side. I founded and ran Chesapeake Compost Works, at the time Maryland’s largest commercial-scale food waste composting facility, so I know what contamination does to a finished product and what farmers and growers need from the soil they buy. That keeps me focused on who ultimately lives with the results of how we handle organic waste and soil.Depackaging is a contested technology, and the scrutiny is fair. Compost that carries plastic into farm fields and gardens undermines the very system it’s meant to support. That’s why I focus on better equipment, measured results, and openness with the farmers, regulators, and communities who care what ends up in their soil.I’m focused on advancing circular economy systems that work — at scale, with staying power. My Founder Story: How My Protect Kit Was Born I started My Protect Kit in the middle of the pandemic, when the world felt upside down and everyone was scrambling for the basics. I was selling masks, gloves, sanitizer, wipes — whatever people needed just to feel safe. But I kept seeing the same thing: People didn’t just need products. They needed preparedness. They needed someone to think ahead for them. That’s when the idea hit me: what if I bundled everything into kits that made life easier? Simple. Practical. Ready for anything. So I launched My Protect Kit out of my parents’ garage in Long Island — surrounded by boxes, stress, and the work ethic my mom and dad drilled into me since I was a kid: if you want something, you work for it… and then you work even harder. Those early days were 18-hour marathons. No days off. No shortcuts. Just grit, belief, and a lot of coffee. But slowly, those kits started spreading across the country. A few hundred became thousands… and now hundreds of thousands globally. Today, My Protect Kit has grown into a brand with one mission: Make life easier by keeping people ready for anything. Travel kits. Everyday kits. Feminine care kits. Beach, ski, baby, dog walk kits — and so many more coming. I didn’t build this with a huge budget or a big corporate background. I built it with heart, hustle, and two parents who taught me that when life gets hard, you don’t quit — you get creative. To everyone who’s supported the journey: thank you. To everyone who’s discovering us now: we’re just getting started. Always ready — because we give a kit. — Darin Milman Founder, My Protect Kit

Chief Marketing and Strategy Officer | Strategic Growth Architect | Creator of the Strategic Orientation Index™ (SOI™)Most companies don’t struggle because they lack a strategy. If you sit in a leadership meeting, things usually make sense. The direction is clear. The priorities are defined. Everyone leaves the room thinking, “we’re aligned.” And then the real work starts. What I’ve seen, over and over again, is that the breakdown doesn’t happen at the level of the plan. It happens in how that plan actually gets interpreted across the organization. Different teams hear the same priority and translate it slightly differently. Decisions that should be straightforward get slowed down or revisited. Customer and market signals don’t land the same way across functions. Nothing breaks all at once. It just does not quite come together. That gap between what we agree to and what we actually do is where strategy starts to drift. That is the problem I have spent my career working on. I am the creator of the Strategic Orientation Index™ (SOI), a behavioral diagnostic that helps organizations see how strategy actually lives inside the business. Not what is written in a plan, but how people think, listen, and act when things get real. Because that is where execution either holds together or does not. In practice, this means helping leadership teams step back and see patterns that are usually invisible from the inside. Where alignment is assumed but not actually consistent. Where good decisions are being made, but not in the same way across the organization. Where growth introduces complexity that starts to create friction. The goal is not to create a better strategy deck. It is to create alignment in behavior so that when the organization moves, it moves coherently. Alongside my work as Chief Marketing and Strategy Officer at KMC Controls and Chief Strategy Officer at KMC Consulting, I have used this lens to help organizations diagnose where execution is breaking down and implement practical changes that improve how decisions get made, how teams coordinate, and how the business responds to the market. I also wrote Strategic Clarity: The Practical Method for Transforming Vision into Results to make this way of thinking more accessible to leaders who feel that gap but do not have a clear way to diagnose it. If you are leading a business and things feel aligned in the room, but inconsistent in reality, that is usually where this work becomes relevant.

We translate technology R&D into implementation — and field realities back into the process. It’s where the science becomes real.Before ICON, I spent over a decade in architectural engineering leading high-performance commercial projects across 8 countries, founded and grew an Austin design studio to a $2M practice, and taught at the university level — all grounded in one belief: technology can only drive change if people want to use it and can trust it.If you’re building at the intersection of construction and technology, or trying to figure out how to make innovative building systems work in practice, I share what I’m learning here.

headline: “The hell I won’t.”It's become something of a personal motto. Tell me something is too ambitious, too complicated, too fast, or that we’ve never done it before, and my first instinct is usually: Okay. I build production capabilities and physical spaces. I figure out equipment, logistics, vendors, budgets and infrastructure. I take on weird problems that don't have an obvious owner. And I spend a lot of time turning “we should do this” into “here's how we're going to do it.”I like ambitious plans. I like building the strategy behind them. But I also believe leadership means being willing to get your hands dirty.I can build the plan, get the right people in the room and make the case to the c-suite, then go downstairs and help the team load the truck if that's what it takes to get the job done. That part of me hasn't changed since I was behind a camera.I don't have much interest in telling talented people what to do from a distance. I want to understand the work, remove the bull*** that gets in their way, give them what they need to be great, and jump in when they need another set of hands.The work I'm most drawn to usually starts with some version of:“We've never done this before.”Good.Let's figure it out.

position: Director, Renewable Energy Sales and Marketing
headline: I build businesses that serve technical experts. Thirty-one years of it: company owner, consultant, then eleven years leading sales and marketing at Apogee Instruments, where our team grew annual revenue many times over by doing one thing relentlessly. Making technical truth easy to buy.Today I lead global sales and marketing for Campbell Scientific’s Renewable Energy division, and I’ll say plainly what most director bios won’t: I was not hired as a utility-scale solar expert. I was hired to help build something. Two years later, it’s built: a division delivering monitoring sensors, stations, and services to utility-scale solar worldwide, run by project managers, system designers, service experts, and sales engineers who act as trusted advisors rather than quota machines. Campbell Scientific earned its measurement reputation over decades, and my job is extending it into this industry until we’re the partner that owners, developers, and EPCs measure everyone else against.The homework is what you’ll see here: weekly posts mapping the real debates in solar performance monitoring. I’m on a deliberate journey to reach the fluency of the best engineers, application experts, and scientists on my own team, and I’m doing it in public. Schools of thought, newest research, pros and cons honestly weighed. And when someone knows more than I do, I hand them the microphone and take notes along with you.To me it’s about arriving at what is right, not who is right. Sometimes that’ll be me. Often it won’t. If a post gets something wrong, say so in the comments. Correcting me isn’t an attack, it’s the whole point. The best discussions on this page happen below the posts, not in them.If you develop, operate, or optimize utility-scale solar, I’m doing this homework in public for you. Follow along, pick a side in the debates, and tell me where I’m wrong, whatever company, role, or region you’re coming from.Yes, people really call me Maddog. It started as a play on Madsen and stuck once people saw how I go after a problem: teeth in until the numbers make sense. I’m friendlier than it sounds.A note on AI, since a couple friends have asked. Yes, my posts get some AI help, the same way they get help from Google, NREL and IEA reports, whatever I can dig up on ResearchGate, and what I can get from picking the brains of the technical geniuses I work with day to day here at Campbell Scientific. I do the digging and the learning. AI helps me cram a week of notes into LinkedIn's 3,000-character limit and fixes my notorious typos. The research and the opinions are mine.

headline: Most high-volume dealerships don’t stop growing because they run out of customers. They stop growing because they run out of capacity.⠀When I took over Rydell Apple Valley Ford Lincoln, it was already a top-30 Ford store selling about 400 vehicles a month, but growth had stalled. The lot was full, recon was slow, and a busy Saturday topped out around 35 deals.⠀We rebuilt the deal workflow and used-car recon process, and connected systems that didn't talk to each other so a deal was entered once instead of three times. In each of my four years there, the dealership exceeded its previous record for annual net profit.⠀That's the work I love most: finding the constraint holding a successful store back and removing it.⠀The hardest part is rarely the process. It's getting a proud, winning team to change how they work. I learned that the hard way. Leading the Document and Mail Automation sales organization at OPEX means I spend my days with organizations sitting on decades of records in boxes, filing cabinets, and back rooms, trying to figure out what to actually do about them.  Here is what I’ve learned. When people price out digitizing their old records, they look at the scan. The scan is the cheap part. The real cost is everything that happens before a page ever reaches a scanner: the pulling, the sorting, the unfolding, and the repairing, done by hand, over and over. Most teams have never put a number on that labor, so it just disappears into payroll.  And it matters more now than it used to, because of AI. Everybody wants to point these new tools at their own information, and they keep hitting the same wall. The information is still on paper. And no matter how hard you try, you cannot run AI on a filing cabinet.  I don’t believe there is one “right way” through this. Some organizations want to rethink the whole workflow. Others just need the paper turned into something usable without breaking what already works. Both are fine. The only thing that does NOT work is pretending the boxes in the basement aren’t a problem.  If you are wrestling with a backfile, a compliance retrieval headache, or just too much paper between you and where you want your operation to go, I am happy to talk. Even if you’re years away from doing anything about it. Nothing in this business is ever truly dead.

I believe organizations are increasing the velocity of transformation faster than they are increasing their capacity to absorb it.The strategy can be sound, the technology can work, and the roadmap looks great on paper.But transformation doesn't happen on paper.It happens inside organizations balancing operational demands, competing priorities, legacy systems, limited capacity, new technology, and people trying to understand what it means for a typical Tuesday.That's the space I've spent much of my career navigating.I'm an enterprise technology and transformation leader with more than a decade of experience turning strategy into execution. I've led complex technology initiatives, digital transformation, organizational change, and IT integration across multiple acquisitions.That experience has left me increasingly interested in a bigger question: How do we build organizations that can continuously transform without outrunning their people?My work explores that question at the intersection of:• Enterprise transformation & strategy execution• AI & the emerging digital workforce• Organizational capacity & change saturation• Technology, operating models, & ways of working• Leadership through uncertainty• The human signals we often label as "resistance"One of my core beliefs is that resistance is information.Questions, hesitation, frustration, disengagement, or capacity concerns aren't simply obstacles. They're often signals about the system we're asking people to operate within.Our job as leaders is to learn how to decode them.That thinking led me to found Change Decoded, where I turn lessons from real-world transformation into practical frameworks, tools, and resources for leaders and practitioners.It's also where I developed the Transformation Harmony Framework & Resistance Decoder work that examines how vision, people, technology, and pace interact, and what organizations tell us when those elements fall out of alignment.Through Leading Change Inside and Out, I explore another side of transformation: what this work asks of the people leading it.And now AI is raising the stakes.As technology moves from supporting work to increasingly performing it, leaders will need to rethink trust, accountability, decision rights, organizational capacity, and even what work looks like.I don't believe the future of transformation will be won simply by organizations that adopt technology fastest.It will belong to organizations that build the capacity to continuously adapt alongside it.And that's the conversation I'm here to explore.

The book lays out an operating model for diagnosing where misalignment is draining revenue, building the infrastructure that turns alignment into daily execution, and embedding alignment into how the business runs normally.
